solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Old man of vigour and energy can’t work after an hour

indicators.note: Something that comes after another follows it, so the work is placed behind the hour.

explanation.surface: An energetic old fellow who nonetheless downs tools after sixty minutes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old man' sounds like a father or an elderly gent, but here it is prehistoric man, and 'can’t work' is not a phrase about idleness but two separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Pithecanthropus, 'ape-man', was the old genus name for Java Man, an early human, so 'old man' is meant in the evolutionary sense.

clue.text: Farmworkers short of new books for colouring

indicators.note: To be short of something is to lack it, so the N is taken away.

blocks.note: pigmen tend pigs on a farm
NT = New Testament, a set of books

explanation.surface: Farm hands too short of new books to have anything but colouring books.
explanation.walkthrough: PIGMEN is a rare but fair word for pig farmworkers. The books are the New Testament, a standard crossword source of NT (and OT).
explanation.definitionFit: A pigment is a substance used to give colour, so it is colouring in the paint-box sense of the noun.

clue.text: One who takes time replacing constant aspect of leader

indicators.note: To replace something is to take its place, so T goes in where the constant was.

blocks.note: CHIEF, a leader, with its C (the symbol for a constant, as in the speed of light) taken out

explanation.surface: Someone patient enough to change one steady trait of the boss.
explanation.walkthrough: C is the standard symbol for a constant, especially the speed of light; 'aspect of leader' marks it as a part of the word for leader.
explanation.definitionFit: A thief takes what is not theirs; the definition is a playful description rather than a dictionary synonym.

clue.text: Bug drove apes mad

indicators.note: Mad means crazy, out of order, so the letters are to be jumbled.

explanation.surface: Some insect has driven a troop of apes crazy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bug' reads as an insect, the pest driving the apes mad, but it is the verb for planting a listening device.
explanation.definitionFit: To bug a room is to eavesdrop on it with a hidden microphone, a spying sense of the verb.

clue.text: Spots cases of academic non-compliance

indicators.note: A case encloses its contents, so a word's case is its outer shell, the first and last letters.

blocks.note: first and last letters of ACADEMIC
first and last letters of NON-COMPLIANCE

explanation.surface: Someone identifies a few instances of a university failing to follow the rules.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spots' looks like a verb meaning notices, and 'cases' like instances; both are something else.
explanation.definitionFit: Acne is the skin condition that brings out spots, pimples, so the answer names the complaint by its symptom.

clue.text: Unusually, he paints and he acts

definitions.note: a clause standing for 'one who acts'

indicators.note: Something done unusually is done in a way out of the normal order, so the letters are rearranged.

explanation.surface: A multi-talented man who is both a painter and an actor.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a little clause: a thespian is someone who acts, so 'he acts' describes him.
explanation.definitionFit: Thespian, from Thespis of ancient Greek drama, is a jokey-formal word for an actor, one who acts.

clue.text: Partially popularise reed pipe

indicators.note: Partially means in part, so only part of the following words is used.

blocks.note: the letters straddle the end of popularise and the start of reed

explanation.surface: An instruction to make a reed pipe somewhat more popular.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reed pipe' looks like a single instrument, but the definition is just 'pipe', and the reed only supplies a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: In plumbing a riser is a vertical pipe carrying water or gas upward through a building, a technical sense of the word.

clue.text: Bargain over pants suit material

indicators.note: To turn something over is to flip it, so the bargain is read backwards.

blocks.note: a snip is British for a bargain
pants and tripe both mean rubbish in British slang

explanation.surface: Haggling over the price of trousers and a suit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pants' is British slang for nonsense, as is tripe, not trousers, though trousers fit the tailoring picture perfectly.
explanation.definitionFit: Pinstripe is cloth with fine stripes, the classic material of a City business suit.

clue.text: Solicitor General holding tongue in row

indicators.note: To hold something is to have it inside your grasp, so SG goes round the tongue.

blocks.note: Hindi is a language, a tongue

explanation.surface: A senior government lawyer biting his tongue during an argument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Holding tongue' suggests keeping quiet, but 'tongue' is a language; 'row' (rhymes with cow) is a noisy quarrel, not a line.
explanation.definitionFit: Besides a lively party, a shindig can be a noisy disturbance, a row, in informal British use.

clue.text: Complaint resolved, given care

indicators.note: To resolve is also to break something down into its parts, so the letters are taken apart and reassembled.

explanation.surface: A complaint that was sorted out because someone took care over it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Resolved' reads as settled, which suits a complaint, but here it means broken down and rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A grievance is a formal complaint about unfair treatment, a plain synonym.

clue.text: Naked musician lying about place in Egypt

indicators.note: Naked means stripped of its covering, so the word loses its outer letters.
About means turned round, so the stripped word lies the other way.

blocks.note: PIANIST stripped of its first and last letters

explanation.surface: An unclothed musician lounging around somewhere in Egypt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lying about' pictures a lazy musician, but it signals a turnaround; the musician is a pianist.
explanation.definitionFit: Sinai is Egypt's peninsula between the Gulfs of Suez and Aqaba, home of Mount Sinai, so a place in Egypt.

clue.text: Whimsical angle on origins of English language

indicators.note: A word's origin is where it starts, so each word gives its first letter.
In an across clue, one thing on another comes after it.

blocks.note: first letters of English and Language

explanation.surface: A playful take on where the English language came from.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Angle' reads as a viewpoint, the angle on a subject, but it is the verb to fish with a rod.
explanation.definitionFit: Elfish means like an elf, mischievous and fanciful, so whimsical by way of fairy-tale character.

clue.text: Acted over appalling red tape

indicators.note: Something appalling is dreadful, a mess, so the letters are scrambled.

explanation.surface: Someone took action about some dreadful bureaucracy.
explanation.walkthrough: O for over comes from cricket scorecards, an over being a set of six balls; 'over' looks like 'about' here but is a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Operated and acted are both past tenses meaning functioned or worked, as a machine or an agent does.

clue.text: Russian cheers master artist

blocks.note: ta = thanks, cheers, in British English

explanation.surface: A Russian toasting a great painter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cheers' looks like a toast, but in British English it is also a casual thank-you, as is ta.
explanation.definitionFit: Tamara is a common Russian woman's name, so a Russian could be a Tamara: a definition by example.

clue.text: I nip round with endless dope for festival

indicators.note: To go round is to turn back on yourself, so I and the nip are read in reverse.
Endless means without an end, so the last letter goes.

blocks.note: a nip and a dram are both small measures of spirits
GRASS, slang for cannabis, without its last letter

explanation.surface: Someone who sneaks a crafty drink and a smoke at a festival.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nip round' suggests popping out on an errand; nip is the drink. 'Dope' is slang for cannabis, which is also called grass.
explanation.definitionFit: Mardi Gras, French for Fat Tuesday, is the carnival before Lent, famous in New Orleans and Rio: a festival by name.

clue.text: King embraced by favourite in the night

indicators.note: To be embraced is to be held in someone's arms, so K sits inside the favourite.

explanation.surface: A king held tight by his beloved during the night.
explanation.walkthrough: Darkling is a poetic word, known from Keats and from Hardy's 'The Darkling Thrush'; the romantic surface suits its register.
explanation.definitionFit: Darkling is a literary adverb and adjective meaning in the dark, a poetic sense rarely met outside verse.

clue.text: Tree dweller fell on a dog, one hears

blocks.note: to KO (knock out) someone is to fell them
a lab is a Labrador dog
an ear is the thing one hears with

explanation.surface: A tree-dweller that tumbled onto a dog, or so they say.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One hears' looks like a sound-alike signal, but it is the ear itself. 'Fell' is a verb meaning knock down, not a hill or the past of fall.
explanation.definitionFit: The koala lives almost entirely in eucalyptus trees in Australia, so it is a tree dweller by habit.

clue.text: Disorder in peninsula’s interior doubled

indicators.note: The interior is the inside, so only the inner letters of the peninsula are kept.
Doubled means made twice over, so the same letters appear two times.

explanation.surface: Unrest in the middle of a peninsula has got twice as bad.
explanation.walkthrough: The peninsula is Iberia, Spain and Portugal together. 'Disorder' is an illness, not unrest.
explanation.definitionFit: Beriberi is a disease caused by lack of vitamin B1, and a disorder is a medical condition.

clue.text: High pace of ebbing sea behind topless couples

indicators.note: Topless means without a top, so the first letter goes.
An ebbing tide flows back, so the sea is read backwards.
Behind means following, so the sea comes after the couples.

blocks.note: 'the deep' is a poetic name for the sea

explanation.surface: Waves retreating behind a pair of sunbathers without tops.
explanation.walkthrough: The sea is 'the deep' in poetry, here as plural DEEPS; 'High pace' sounds like hurry, but the height is literal.
explanation.definitionFit: Airspeed is an aircraft's speed relative to the air, a pace measured high up, hence the cryptic hint of 'high'.

clue.text: Retired agents eating nasty pasty

indicators.note: To retire is to withdraw, go back, so the whole assembly is read backwards (up, in a down clue).
Something eating food takes it inside, so CIA goes round MEAN.

blocks.note: the CIA, the US intelligence agency

explanation.surface: Spies who have retired eating a disgusting Cornish pasty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pasty' is the adjective meaning pale, not the pastry (a pasty is a British meat-and-vegetable pie).
explanation.definitionFit: Anaemia leaves the skin pale, so someone anaemic looks pasty: the definition works by symptom.

clue.text: Pet worries son

explanation.surface: A pet animal is a source of anxiety to a boy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pet' looks like a noun, the animal, but it is the verb to stroke.
explanation.definitionFit: Pet as a verb means stroke fondly, a plain synonym of caress.

clue.text: Observe nurses caught with liquor and cider

indicators.note: To nurse something is to hold it close, cradled, so SPY goes round the rest.

explanation.surface: Watching nurses being caught drinking spirits and cider.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nurses' looks like hospital staff, but it is the verb meaning hold close.
explanation.definitionFit: Scrumpy is the rough, strong farmhouse cider of south-west England, a regional kind of cider.

clue.text: Pilot advanced by means of broadcast stunts

indicators.note: Something broadcast is put out on air, heard rather than seen, so the stunts are spelt by their sound.

blocks.note: stunts are tricks, spelt by their sound

explanation.surface: A pilot got ahead by doing daredevil stunts on air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broadcast' only covers the last piece; the first two are plain charade.
explanation.definitionFit: Aviatrix is the dated feminine form of aviator, so a woman pilot.

clue.text: Name of strict elder ignoring those in odd positions

indicators.note: Ignoring the odd-numbered letters leaves the even ones, every second letter.

explanation.surface: The name of a severe church elder, skipping the odd ones out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Odd' pictures the elder's eccentric flock, but it means odd-numbered.
explanation.definitionFit: A title is the name of a book, film or song, a plain synonym.

clue.text: Leader who nationalised waterway and space agency in speech

indicators.note: In speech means spoken, so the space agency's name is taken as a sound.

blocks.note: NASA, the US space agency, in a non-rhotic British accent

explanation.surface: A leader who took over a canal and also runs a space programme.
explanation.walkthrough: In British speech the final R of NASSER is silent, so it matches NASA. The definition is the long first half.
explanation.definitionFit: Gamal Abdel Nasser, Egypt's president, nationalised the Suez Canal in 1956, prompting the Suez Crisis.

clue.text: Hit creepy-crawlies when cycling

indicators.note: Cycling means going round in a loop, so the last letter comes round to the front.

explanation.surface: Swatting at bugs while out on a bike ride.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cycling' looks like bike riding, but it means rotating the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Smite is an old, biblical-sounding verb for strike hard, a literary synonym of hit.

clue.text: Drains backed up in health resorts

indicators.note: Backed means going backwards, and up is the reverse direction in a down clue.

explanation.surface: Blocked drains at a health resort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drains backed up' reads as a plumbing problem; drains is the verb saps.
explanation.definitionFit: Spas, named after the Belgian town of Spa, are places with mineral springs or treatments for health.

clue.text: Retrospective component of entire market value

indicators.note: A retrospective looks backwards, so the letters are read in reverse.
A component is a part, so the letters are a part of the phrase that follows.

blocks.note: the last four letters of entire and the first of market

explanation.surface: A look back at one part of a company's total market valuation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Market value' looks like the definition; only 'value' is, and 'market' hosts a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Merit means worth, as in judging something on its merits, a plain synonym of value.

clue.text: It could be used for sex?

definitions.text: It could be used for sex?

blocks.note: surface reading: an object, some sex aid; setter's reading: a word that could be employed
surface reading: for the act; setter's reading: in place of the word 'sex'

explanation.surface: Something that might be employed for sex, like a toy.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue invites a racy reading; 'used for' means said instead of, as a polite word stands in for sex.
explanation.definitionFit: A euphemism is a mild word used in place of a blunt one, like 'intimacy' or 'relations' for sex.

clue.text: It artificially corrects my guise

indicators.note: Something done artificially is contrived, not natural, so the letters are rearranged by hand.

blocks.note: the subject of the &lit reading, not wordplay

explanation.surface: Someone describing how a procedure fixes their appearance.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition, and all but 'It' is also the wordplay: the letters are rearranged just as the face is.
explanation.definitionFit: Read straight, the clue describes exactly what cosmetic surgery does: it artificially alters someone's appearance.
